summary: Describes version 2 of the Open Network Computing Remote Procedure Call protocol as deployed, which lets a program call a procedure on another machine as if it were local. It obsoletes RFC 1831 and was on the standards track as a Draft Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Remote Procedure Call lets one computer ask another to run a task, like calling a helper from another room. This note writes down the rules for how those requests and answers look.

subtitle: How one program calls a procedure on another machine, and how the call, the reply and the errors are laid out on the wire.

tldr.problem: Programs on different machines need a common way to call procedures on each other, identify the procedure, match replies to calls and say who is calling.
tldr.mechanism: ONC RPC version 2 defines a call message and a reply message in the XDR language. A call names a program, version and procedure and carries a credential and a verifier. A reply says whether the call was accepted or denied, and why.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5531 is the authoritative description of RPC version 2 and obsoletes RFC 1831 without changing the wire protocol. It is a Draft Standard and has since been updated by RFC 9289.

today: RFC 5531 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 1831, and it has been updated by RFC 9289. It remains the definition of the RPC version 2 message protocol, and the RFC states that it adds no over-the-wire changes compared with RFC 1831.

sections.title: What RFC 5531 Specifies
sections.content:
RFC 5531 specifies version 2 of the message protocol used in ONC Remote Procedure Call (RPC). The messages are described in the XDR language of RFC 4506, and the RFC assumes the reader already knows XDR. It does not try to justify RPC systems or describe their use.

The abstract says the document describes RPC version 2 as it is currently deployed and accepted. It obsoletes RFC 1831 as the authoritative description, without introducing any over-the-wire protocol changes.

The changes from RFC 1831 are mostly administrative: an appendix and an IANA Considerations section describe how program numbers, authentication flavor numbers and authentication status numbers are requested from IANA instead of from Sun Microsystems. The RPC language specification is clarified to match current usage, the Security Considerations are enhanced, and new authentication errors that are in common use are specified.
sections.plainLanguage: This note is the official rulebook for asking another computer to run a job for you. It was already how people did it; the note just makes the rules official and says who hands out the job numbers.

sections.title: The RPC Model and Its Transports
sections.content:
A network service is a collection of one or more remote programs. A program implements one or more procedures, and a server may support more than one version of a program so it can stay compatible as protocols change. The terms client and server apply only to a particular transaction, so one host or process can play both roles at different times.

The model mirrors a local procedure call. The caller sends a call message carrying the procedure's parameters and waits for a reply message carrying the results. The RFC points out that this is only an example: the protocol places no restriction on the concurrency model, so calls may be asynchronous or the server may start a separate task per call.

Remote calls differ from local ones in four ways the RFC lists: error handling (server or network failure), no global variables or side effects across address spaces, performance (usually orders of magnitude slower), and authentication, since calls may cross unsecured networks.

RPC defines only the messages, not how they travel. It does not implement reliability. Over TCP most of the work is done for the application, but over UDP the application must implement its own time-out, retransmission and duplicate detection. A server can use the transaction ID (xid) to remember granted requests and get some degree of execute-at-most-once behavior, but it may examine the ID only as a test for equality. Over TCP a reply means the procedure ran exactly once, but no reply tells the client nothing, so time-outs and reconnections are still needed. Binding a client to a service is explicitly not part of this specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Asking a faraway helper to do a job is like asking someone in the next room, except the helper might not answer and the message might get lost. RPC only decides how the notes look; the postal service you pick decides whether they arrive.

sections.title: The Call and Reply Messages
sections.content:
Every RPC message starts with a transaction identifier, xid, followed by a two-armed union whose discriminant is msg_type: CALL (0) or REPLY (1). The xid of a reply always matches the call that started it. It is used only by clients to match replies to calls and by servers to detect retransmissions; the server cannot treat it as a sequence number.

A call body holds rpcvers (which MUST equal 2), then prog, vers and proc naming the remote program, its version and the procedure, then the credential cred and verifier verf, and finally the procedure-specific parameters.

A reply is either MSG_ACCEPTED (0) or MSG_DENIED (1). An accepted reply begins with a verifier that the server generates to validate itself to the client, followed by an accept_stat value. SUCCESS is followed by procedure-specific results, PROG_MISMATCH carries the lowest and highest supported program versions, and the other values carry nothing. A denied reply is either RPC_MISMATCH, which carries the lowest and highest supported RPC versions, or AUTH_ERROR, which carries an auth_stat value saying why authentication failed.

Calls can fail even when accepted. A server that has the program but not the version, or cannot decode the parameters, still answers with a reply that explains what went wrong.
sections.plainLanguage: Every note starts with a number so you can tell which question an answer belongs to. A question names the job, which edition of the job, and who is asking. The answer says either the result or exactly why the helper could not do it.

sections.title: Authentication Flavors
sections.content:
A call carries two authentication fields, the credential and the verifier, and a reply carries one response verifier. All three have the type opaque_auth: an auth_flavor number followed by up to 400 bytes that RPC itself does not interpret. The flavors listed are AUTH_NONE (0), AUTH_SYS (1), AUTH_SHORT (2), AUTH_DH (3) and RPCSEC_GSS (6), with more to be defined.

Null authentication (AUTH_NONE) is mandatory: it MUST be available in all implementations. It is for calls where the client does not care about its identity or the server does not care who the client is, and the RFC recommends zero-length opaque data. Implementors MAY include AUTH_SYS to support existing applications.

AUTH_SYS (Appendix A) sends a structure with an arbitrary stamp, the caller's machinename (up to 255 characters), its effective uid and gid, and up to 16 supplementary gids. The server may reply with an AUTH_SHORT verifier, a shorthand the client can send in place of the full credential to save bandwidth and server CPU. If the server flushes it, the call is rejected with AUTH_REJECTEDCRED and the client may fall back to the full credential.

The auth_stat codes explain failures, for example AUTH_BADCRED (1), AUTH_REJECTEDCRED (2), AUTH_BADVERF (3), AUTH_REJECTEDVERF (4) and AUTH_TOOWEAK (5). Later values cover Kerberos-related errors, which are marked deprecated, and two RPCSEC_GSS errors, 13 and 14.
sections.plainLanguage: Each note has a little box for proving who you are. The box can be empty, can say your name and your group like a school ID, or can hold stronger proof. If the helper does not like the proof, it tells you which part was wrong.

sections.title: Program Numbers and IANA
sections.content:
Three unsigned integers in the call, the program number, the version number and the procedure number, uniquely identify what is being called. A first implementation would most likely use version 1, but the version MUST NOT be zero. Procedure meanings are documented in each program's own specification; the RFC's example is a file service where procedure 5 is read and procedure 12 is write. By convention, procedure 0 of any RPC protocol has the same semantics and never requires authentication.

The 32-bit program number space is divided into blocks, shown in the table. Section 13 hands authority over program numbers, authentication flavor numbers and auth_stat numbers from Sun Microsystems to IANA, and preserves Sun's earlier assignments, which were in the decimal range 100000 to 399999. IANA begins its own assignments at 400000, first come first served. Appendix C lists the current assignments, such as the portmapper at 100000 and NFS at 100003.

Blocks of numbers within the IANA range are granted by size: up to 100 numbers first come first served, up to 1000 with a specification required, and more than 1000 with IESG approval. Existing RPCSEC_GSS pseudo-flavors for NFS were granted in the decimal range 390000 to 390255.
sections.plainLanguage: Every job has a number, like a phone extension, so the caller can ask for exactly the right one. A central office hands out extensions so two companies never get the same one, and some blocks are kept for private or temporary use.

sections.title: Record Marking over Byte Streams
sections.content:
A byte-stream transport such as TCP does not mark where one message ends and the next begins. RPC therefore defines record marking: one RPC message fits into one record, and a record is made of one or more record fragments.

Each fragment starts with a four-byte header followed by from 0 up to 231 minus 1 bytes of fragment data. The header is an unsigned number in network byte order that encodes two things: the highest-order bit says whether this is the last fragment of the record (1 means last), and the 31 low-order bits give the fragment's length in bytes. The RFC notes that this record format is not in standard XDR form.

Batching and broadcast are two other uses described in the RFC. In batching, the client sends many calls without waiting and the server sends no replies, usually over a reliable stream, ending with a normal call to flush the pipeline. In broadcast, the client sends one call to the network and waits for numerous replies, which needs a packet-based transport such as UDP; such servers usually answer only when the call succeeds.
sections.plainLanguage: When messages flow down a pipe one after another, you need a marker to show where each one stops. RPC puts a small label in front of each piece saying how long it is and whether it is the last piece.

sections.title: The RPC Language
sections.content:
The RPC language is an extension of the XDR language, adding program, version and procedure declarations. The keywords program and version are reserved. A program definition holds one or more version definitions, and each version holds one or more procedure definitions, each assigned an unsigned constant.

The RFC's example is a ping program, PING_PROG, with a latest version PING_VERS_PINGBACK (version 2) and an original version PING_VERS_ORIG (version 1). Procedure 0, PINGPROC_NULL, takes nothing and returns nothing and is useful for measuring round-trip time. PINGPROC_PINGBACK, procedure 1, makes the server ping the client back and return the elapsed microseconds.

Syntax notes: a version or procedure name or number cannot appear twice within its scope, and current compilers generally do not support more than one type in a procedure argument list, so the usual practice is to wrap arguments in a structure.
sections.plainLanguage: The RPC language is a way to write a menu of jobs a helper can do, with a number beside each one and a version for each menu, so both sides read the same list.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
AUTH_SYS is known to be insecure because it has no verifier that lets the credential be validated. It SHOULD NOT be used for services that permit clients to modify data, and it MUST NOT be specified as RECOMMENDED or REQUIRED for any Standards Track RPC service. AUTH_DH is considered obsolete and insecure, with the same restrictions.

The RFC points to RPCSEC_GSS (RFC 2203), which lets GSS-API mechanisms secure RPC, and says all non-trivial RPC programs developed in the future should implement RPCSEC_GSS-based security appropriately. Standards Track RPC services MUST mandate support for RPCSEC_GSS and for an authentication pseudo-flavor with levels of security suited to the need for simple authentication, integrity or data privacy.

Appendix A adds that AUTH_SYS can be considered legitimate only when applications and the network can be secured externally and privileged transport addresses are used, such as privileged ports on UNIX systems, which not all systems enforce.
sections.plainLanguage: The simplest ID in this system is just a name tag anyone can write, so it should never guard anything important. The stronger options are like proper locks, and new official services have to support them.
